articles.author: Nurbek Bekmurzaev
articles.title: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, children with Down syndrome are using a video game to safely navigate the internet
articles.excerpt: A virtual assistant called Sol the Owl guides kids through the game
articles.content:
This story by Nurbek Bekmurzaev originally appeared on Global Voices. Text licensed under CC BY 3.0. Reformatted for reading; third-party media omitted.

A virtual assistant called Sol the Owl guides kids through the game

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement. 

Like their peers, children and young people with Down syndrome are curious about technology and the internet, but there are often no suitable, dedicated tools to help them learn how to safely navigate the web. This is true in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well, where children with cognitive disabilities are underserved and tend to end up in digital isolation because of caregivers’ concerns about digital safety and the risks of being online.

There are approximately 550-700 children and adolescents with Down syndrome in the country. They are supported by three specialized associations nationwide: the Association “Life with Down Syndrome of FBiH”, Down Syndrome Association Mostar, and DOWN SY I MI. To teach online safety, these organizations have to rely on online safety tools that heavily feature text, abstract explanations, and complex language, which are not accessible or meaningful for children with Down syndrome.

A group of developers, IT professionals, and designers in Bosnia and Herzegovina has been working to address the lack of a digital safety tool tailored to children and adolescents with Down syndrome. Their goal is to help young people understand, practice, and feel confident making decisions online.

Global Voices conducted a written interview over email with Stefan Filipovic, a member of this group, to learn how they created a video game to teach children with the genetic condition about digital safety. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Stefan Filipovic (SF): We are a group of IT professionals, developers, and designers from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Most of our work is in commercial technology, but we also have experience developing educational and socially useful video games, such as Eureka – Edukativna videoigra, an educational game for children, and Lea & Leo, a game about children with diabetes.

We joined the Digital Sparks project because we wanted to use that experience for a group that, in our opinion, is often overlooked when digital products are designed. Young people with intellectual disabilities are using phones and the internet, but many digital tools are simply not designed with their needs in mind.

The video game SafeClick (Siguran klik) allowed us to work on something practical and useful while also learning how to design more inclusively and to involve educators and users in the process.

GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

SF: While working with Servis Centar “Dajte nam šansu – Zvjezdice” – an association and day center that provides free support to children, young people, and people with developmental disabilities, we saw that young people with Down syndrome were using phones and the internet, but there were very few cyber-safety resources made specifically for them.

Most materials use a lot of text, complicated explanations, or interfaces that are difficult to follow. To our knowledge, parents and educators often end up focusing on limiting internet use rather than teaching young people how to deal with unsafe situations.

We wanted to try something different. With SafeClick, we use simple stories, familiar situations, pictures, and game mechanics to help users practice what to do when they receive a suspicious message, meet someone online, or experience cyberbullying.

GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

SF: We developed the first playable version of SafeClick. The game is currently awaiting approval by the App Store and Google Play. It is designed for mobile devices, with simple, accessible interactions and visual scenarios.

One important decision was to avoid punishing users for mistakes. Instead, the game explains what happened and gives them another chance. We worked closely with educators and parents and used their feedback to make the scenarios easier to understand.

We are currently in the phase of arranging mentoring sessions with the mentor assigned to us through the project, with the aim of earning additional opportunities to promote the game and  reach as many users as possible.

GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples. 

SF: Although the game will  be published soon, the initial feedback from special education teachers and parents has been highly practical. Special thanks to Jelena Zilic and her children, who provided the first useful in-game test users’ feedback. They helped us see that situations, which are difficult to explain verbally, can become much easier when they are shown visually and practiced through a game.

For example, instead of simply telling someone not to respond to a stranger online, SafeClick lets them see the message, decide what to do, and practice blocking and reporting that individual, and reporting the situation to a caregiver. I really believe we managed to turn an abstract topic into something young people can actually practice.

GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed?

SF: Before this project, we mostly thought about accessibility as a product and UX (interface) issue. Working on SafeClick made us look at it differently. Being able to use the internet safely is also about being able to participate in everyday life. Communicate, learn, find information, and be part of your community.

If a person cannot understand or safely use digital services, they are left out. We also learned that privacy and accessibility should not be things added at the end of development. They need to be considered from the beginning. That is something we will take with us into our future projects.

GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

SF: The biggest lesson for us was that making something technically simple is actually quite difficult. With commercial products, it is easy to keep adding features. With SafeClick, we had to constantly ask ourselves whether a button, animation, sentence, or screen was really necessary.

Our earlier experience with Eureka – Edukativna igra and Lea & Leo helped us understand the value of video games for learning, but SafeClick taught us much more about cognitive accessibility and designing with educators and users in mind.

GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

SF: Our immediate objective is to publish SafeClick, launch it in the media, and inform the wider community about the game’s availability. Looking ahead, we plan to build on this experience to develop a wider portfolio of digital tools tailored for marginalized groups and to continue exploring how games and other digital tools can make learning and participation easier for people who are often left out of mainstream technology. We are open to new collaborations and partnerships.

Written by Nurbek Bekmurzaev

articles.author: Peter Dizikes | MIT News
articles.title: At MIT, Martha Minow speaks on sustaining democracy, both by using and overcoming AI
articles.excerpt: In Compton Lecture, the distinguished legal scholar warns of potential “loss of the Enlightenment” while suggesting ways innovations can meet our civic and cultural needs.
articles.content:
Peter Dizikes | MIT News · MIT News · MIT News republication policy

In Compton Lecture, the distinguished legal scholar warns of potential “loss of the Enlightenment” while suggesting ways innovations can meet our civic and cultural needs.

Legal scholar Martha Minow delivered this fall’s Compton Lecture at MIT on Thursday, examining the civic foundations of democracy — and describing how artificial intelligence is undermining it, but could be used to help reinforce traditional U.S. governance. 

“It’s not a good time for democracy or constitutionalism,” said Minow, who is the 300th Anniversary University Professor at Harvard University, and a prominent expert in constitutional law and human rights. She noted a litany of challenges to democracy in recent years, including violations of laws and norms, the stifling of free speech, a diminution of congressional authority, disregard of legal rulings, the common vilification of others in society, and more. 

Recent Gallup polling, Minow observed, shows 77 percent of people saying that the founders of the U.S. would be disappointed in the contemporary condition of the country. 

“Many people genuinely wonder whether this nation’s system of government and rule of law, ignited 250 years ago, will survive,” Minow said.  

Her remarks assessed the state of the U.S. in terms of what she called four key “ingredients” of democracy: education, reliable and accessible information, security from violence, and fairness. Minow evaluated how AI has, among other things, influenced these areas of life — but also suggested ways people could use contemporary technology to help. 

“It’s very familiar to hear blame attributed to digital technologies and experts of all stripes, but a turnaround, I believe, is genuinely possible if people at MIT and elsewhere pour time and talent towards real and much-needed solutions,” Minow said. 

A substantial portion of her remarks focused on the pitfalls of AI in education. That issue compounds some other troubling trends: The U.S. already has large local and regional disparities in educational funding, Minow noted, while schools have actually become significantly more segregated in economic and ethnic terms over the last three decades. 

In this context, AI threatens to further weaken independent-thinking skills, Minow suggested, just when greater understanding of civic issues is absolutely vital. 

“As AI surges, I think we have to learn to be smarter about how to use it, how to regulate it, and how to actually educate people about the costs of mindless using,” Minow said. She added: “Dominant AI platforms supercharge the strategies that are deployed by social media companies, inducing passivity in people … Leading AI models and interfaces and sycophantic elements endanger the development particularly of young people’s capabilities to think, to remember, and to engage in critical thinking.” 

That trend away from cognitive effort, she suggested, can be changed — perhaps through AI tools that act more like tutors and are designed to enhance people’s deep thinking.

“Existing LLMs, model training, and interface design can offer nudges and questions and hints rather than replacing student work, but there’s so much more that could be developed, and more effectively, to be trustworthy, and to deepen human activities and curiosity, rather than replacing people,” Minow said.

To the audience, she added, “AI tools could do much more of that … And I believe that you, the people here, could develop better tools than the ones that are out there. And make better assessments, more meaningful and cheating-resistant.” 

Minow’s talk, “Constituting Democracy in the Era of AI,” was delivered to a large audience in MIT’s Huntington Hall, Room 10-250 on campus.

MIT President Sally A. Kornbluth delivered introductory remarks to the audience. The Karl Taylor Compton Lecture Series, introduced in 1957, is the highest-profile event of its kind at MIT. Karl Taylor Compton was MIT’s ninth president, serving from 1930 to 1948, and then becoming chair of the MIT Corporation from 1948 to 1954.

“He guided MIT through the Great Depression and World War II,” Kornbluth said, “transforming the Institute from an outstanding school for training job-ready engineers to a great global research university.” 

She added: “He was also a deeply committed patriot who helped harness the intellectual power of America’s research universities to serve the nation during World War II.” 

Kornbluth called Minow “a legal scholar of extraordinary intellectual scope,” and a “dedicated educator whose work has shaped how we think about the law and our own humanity, as individuals and as a society.” 

Minow has been a faculty member at Harvard Law School since 1981, and served as dean of the school from 2009 through 2017. Minow earned her BA in history from the University of Michigan, an MA in education from Harvard, and a JD from Yale University.

Minow’s books include “Making All the Difference” (1990), “Partners Not Rivals” (2002), and “When Should Law Forgive?” (2020). 

In her talk, Minow also discussed the civic effects of misinformation, threats of violence, and multiple dimension of societal fairness. Modern media technology has led to a 75 percent reduction in journalists in recent decades, Minow observed, with an attendant rise in corruption in places without local media. Civic-minded technologists, she proposed, should work towards establishing a widely-used “information commons,” or many forms of them, to help people access more reliable information. 

Meanwhile, when it comes to basic security in society, Minow warned, “We’re on the brink right now. I know a lot of judges, and every one of them has a credible threat of violence against them. In America. This is not acceptable.” 

For all the challenges to democracy and traditional civic norms, however, Minow sounded positive notes throughout her remarks, pointing out that there are many opportunities to create new forms of reliable information, education, and community relations. 

“We have to actually invent the world that we want to live in,” she offered. 

Minow’s remarks were followed by a Q&A session in which Kornbluth read aloud questions submitted by the audience — and asked her to characterize her concerns about present trends. 

“I worry about the loss of the Enlightenment,” Minow said. “I worry about the loss of the belief that reason, and testing hypotheses, and rejecting myths in the face of evidence, and the toleration and rights and expansion of participation that came along with the Enlightenment, that’s what concerns me the most. That’s why the disinformation issue for me is so important, that’s why the loss of critical thinking in schools is so important.”

She added: “I’ve spent much of my own career thinking about mass violence. What happens when people don’t understand each other, and are afraid. And it’s terrible, and we don’t want to be there. And I do view the Enlightenment as a time when people learned that actually having mass wars is a bad thing, and coming up with toleration is a good thing, and testing our ideas in light of evidence other people can share can produce a better life for everybody. I worry we’re abandoning that right now.”

articles.author: Benjamin Daniel | School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences
articles.title: Reinforcing the value of human understanding at MIT
articles.excerpt: During the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences’ 75th Anniversary Symposium, President Sally Kornbluth said “MIT has never needed your particular insight and guidance more than we do now.”
articles.content:
Benjamin Daniel | School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences · MIT News · MIT News republication policy

During the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences’ 75th Anniversary Symposium, President Sally Kornbluth said “MIT has never needed your particular insight and guidance more than we do now.”

At the MIT School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS) 75th Anniversary Symposium, speakers celebrated the school’s value and contributions, while exploring how artificial intelligence is transforming many aspects of teaching, research, and society.

The symposium was held Sept. 24-25 in the Linde Music Building’s Thomas Tull Concert Hall. Scholars, students, staff, and alumni from across SHASS and MIT gathered for the event, which kicked off with welcoming remarks from MIT leadership. 

“How should we think about MIT’s School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences? With enthusiastic appreciation and gratitude,” said President Sally Kornbluth.

The school’s origins date back to the Lewis Committee Report, commissioned by MIT and published in 1949, which called for stronger integration between scientific and technical topics and humanistic scholarship and teaching.

Kornbluth noted that, much like when the school was founded just after World War II, the world faces uncertainty as it grapples with the broad implications of artificial intelligence.

“AI has suddenly arrived with enormous consequences for both research and education,” she said. “As we face the challenges of our own time, and our own society, it’s clear that MIT has never needed your particular insight and guidance more than we do now.”

In opening remarks, Provost Anantha Chandrakasan described the importance of a human-centered approach to technology, one that considers both its efficacy and its impacts. He lauded many of the new research projects happening through the MIT Human Insight Collaborative, a strategic initiative launched in 2024.

“Today — a time of rapid, AI-driven change — the arts, humanities, and social sciences are as important as ever,” he said. “To be able to contribute effectively to solving the world’s great challenges, it is not enough to gain technical mastery.”

Chancellor Melissa Nobles recalled how, during her tenure as SHASS dean from 2015 to 2021, reading the positive feedback from students in their SHASS course assessments reinforced the value of the school’s teaching.

“MIT students have a range of interests that draw them to our classes that may be invisible to their STEM professors, but that we very well know our students have,” said Nobles, who is also a professor of political science.

Agustín Rayo, the Kenan Sahin Dean of SHASS and professor of philosophy, noted that, while research in the school plays a key role in addressing global issues such as climate change and AI, the value of the work in SHASS should not be measured by practical application alone.

“Education should also help us ask what is worth doing, what do we owe one another, and what makes a life worth living,” Rayo said. “Some research matters because it helps us understand the histories, cultures, and social structures that have made us who we are. Some things matter because they enrich human life.”

Scholarship from across SHASS and beyond 

Over the symposium’s two days, research presentations, panel discussions, and performances offered attendees opportunities to engage with the role of SHASS in exploring today’s biggest societal questions.

“We gather not so much to look back over the past 75 years, but to showcase where we are now, and share what we urgently aim to tackle together in the years ahead,” said David Kaiser, Germeshausen Professor of the History of Science and professor of physics at MIT, who also served as chair of the symposium planning committee.

The first day included a session on teaching and learning innovations. Faculty presented on the success of educational programs housed within SHASS, including the MIT Indigenous Languages Initiative Master's Program, the Master in Data, Economics, and Design of Policy (DEDP), and MISTI, the hub for global experiences for MIT students.

Stephanie Seed, associate professor of literature, spoke about why she and others are working to reintegrate classic books into their teaching.

“MIT, of course, is an institution unusually oriented towards the future,” she said. “Our students are trained to imagine and create worlds that don’t yet exist. And it’s precisely this future orientation that makes reading the past especially important here.”

Eric Klopfer, professor of Comparative Media Studies/Writing and co-author of MIT’s recent report on AI and instruction, said this is a moment when instructors must reassess how courses are taught.

“I don’t know exactly what that looks like, but I do think it means something that’s more than modifying our curriculum. I think it really means rethinking what the educational experience is,” he said.

During a session on computing and society, panelists described different views and research into technology and how it affects humans.

“We project aspects of ourselves onto computational systems,” said MIT Professor D. Fox Harrell during his talk about seeing “selfness” in machines. 

“What makes an AI system is not just the code, not just the programming or the algorithm, it’s the fact that we narrate it as being intentional,” he said.

Program in Science, Technology, and Society Professor Sherry Turkle offered a skeptical view of human-technology interaction, particularly with AI chatbots, which she describes as “intimate machines.” 

“If social media came for our attention, I argue that chatbots are coming for our capacity for attachment, which is deeper and much more troubling,” said Turkle.

Professor David Autor, head of the Department of Economics, said it’s an exciting time to be working at MIT, where scholars are collaborating to explore AI’s impact on society.

“I don’t think there’s a close analogy to a moment when everyone felt the world change so quickly,” he said. “The stakes feel incredibly high.”

Celebrating the arts and engaging with the future 

The first day concluded with a rousing Music and Theater Arts performance showcase, which began with an excerpt from Stan Lai’s “A Dream Like A Dream,” a play directed and performed by students and instructors in class 21T.100 (Theater Arts Production).

“Variations on the Theme of SHASS 75,” a piece choreographed by Dan Safer, senior lecturer and director of dance programs, combined movement, lighting, and music in a celebration of both the human body and the school’s milestone anniversary.

Student and faculty musicians from a variety of styles and disciplines shared the stage, including Rambax MIT, MIT Concert Choir, and the MIT All-Star Jazz Combo. The showcase included stirring renditions of “Madrigal,” composed by Vice Provost for the Arts Keeril Makan, and “Prayer for Peace.”

On the second day of the symposium, several alumni presented on their current work and the impact of their SHASS experiences.

Jessica Coon PhD ’10, now a professor of linguistics at McGill University, spoke about the leading role MIT Linguistics plays in preserving endangered languages, and how her studies at MIT prepared her to carry on that work.

“SHASS gives us the tools not just to conduct research, but to communicate the impacts of this research across a variety of different audiences and in different ways,” she said.

Ankita Reddy ’19 double-majored in anthropology and biology and is now an MD/PhD student at the University of Pennsylvania. She highlighted her most impactful SHASS courses, including 21A.308 (Global Mental Health).

“This was the first time I was forced to consider how good health care looks different based on social systems and cultural practices,” she said. “SHASS made me more comfortable with, and more curious about, complexity.”

During the symposium’s final session, panelists engaged in a conversation about AI, art, and the implications for creatives in an era where their art can be co-opted and copied. 

“There’s so much praise for new and upgraded technologies,” remarked associate professor of literature Sandy Alexandre. “The question I consistently have is: What does it mean to be an upgraded human being? How are we innovating as technology is innovating?”

Philosopher Justin Khoo said AI’s role in art could be considered a “giant paint brush you don’t have much control over,” adding he could see the creation of new sub-genres of art that are human-only, AI-infused, and purely AI, for example.

Khoo closed by saying he encourages students to “think broadly, and really take seriously the humanistic education here at MIT.”

“A broad understanding of a set of concepts which are widely applicable, not just narrowly applicable, I think that’s what we need more than ever now,” he said.

As the symposium came to a close, attendee Kent Sahin praised the event.

“I’ve attended every session, and this is a fantastic program and a great celebration of the 75th anniversary,” he said. “Clearly, whether it’s AI impact, the impact of climate change, or the impact of political and social change, SHASS is in the right place at the right time.”

articles.author: Guest Contributor
articles.title: Complementary forces: Why activism needs art to drive action
articles.excerpt: ‘A striking action, a touch of humor, or an unexpected scene can attract attention.’
articles.content:
This story by Guest Contributor originally appeared on Global Voices. Text licensed under CC BY 3.0. Reformatted for reading; third-party media omitted.

‘A striking action, a touch of humor, or an unexpected scene can attract attention.’

This post is by Nikola Pisarev, an art historian and a pioneer of creative activism in North Macedonia, who serves as the program director at the Contemporary Art Center in Skopje. It is also part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

In recent decades, practices that bring art directly into people’s everyday lives have become increasingly common. They may be initiated by artists, activists, informal groups, or citizens who use creative means to draw attention to a problem, express disagreement, or call for change. Public spaces become a place where an action meets an audience, provokes a response, and starts a conversation. This approach, when artistic and creative means are used to press for solutions or encourage social change, is called artistic activism.

At their core, art and activism have different but complementary roles. Activism seeks to change a situation through strategic planning and advocacy; art, on the other hand, is not pro or against but can move people emotionally.

Art can change how people see and experience a situation. It opens up new perspectives and associations, and its effects are not always immediate or easy to measure. Artistic activism brings these possibilities together: It uses the emotional experience of art as a prompt for action and directs that action towards change.

Urban art actions in North Macedonia offer local examples for exploring this approach. Many actions were developed through direct engagement with specific problems, rather than as part of a broader methodology. They began with a desire to point out an injustice, raise a question, or help address a problem.

What makes artistic activism compelling?

It does not always take a large crowd to draw attention to a problem. A striking action, a touch of humor, or an unexpected scene can attract attention even when it is created by a small group — or by a single person. This does not replace the power of mass organizing, but it makes action possible when resources are limited.

Additionally, amid the constant barrage of information, an unusual sculpture, a witty message, or an intervention in public space can interrupt people’s routine scrolling. They may photograph and share the action, extending its reach beyond the place where it took place through social media and communication platforms.

Still, a high number of views does not mean the problem has been solved. Visibility is an opportunity that needs to be connected to the action’s purpose.

Within high-risk or authoritarian contexts, creative action can also give activists greater room to act, even under pressure. Humor, metaphor, and unexpected forms can sometimes make a problem visible without direct confrontation. In some cases, the people behind an action can also remain anonymous. This does not make them immune to pressure: The level of risk depends on the context, the subject, and the way the action is carried out. But a creative form may allow organizers to absorb some of that pressure while keeping the affected community less exposed.

Likewise, a problem hidden in reports, procedures, or individual experiences can remain invisible to the larger public. An artistic action can translate a complex situation into an image, object, or scene that people can readily recognize. This can encourage citizens, experts and decision-makers to discuss the problem and possible solutions. The challenge is to make the message clear without distorting the substance of the issue.

Art also has a way of enduring long after it has disappeared from public space. A scene, symbol, or object can become a story that the media and the public continue to share after the intervention has ended.

The people behind an action do not need to specialize in every aspect of the problem. They do need to understand its core, use reliable information, and listen to those directly affected.

There are countless ways artistic activism can affect a community. It might prompt an immediate response from the authorities, change how people see an issue, or encourage other social actors to get involved.

Immediate response and problem-solving

Some actions prompt the authorities to respond quickly. This most often happens with concrete local infrastructure problems: potholes, broken streetlights, faults in water or electricity networks, and smaller environmental issues.

North Macedonia has seen many examples: “The Guinness World Record for the Longest Road Construction”; rubber ducklings placed in the mud at the entrance to a kindergarten in Štip; “fishing” for potholes in Veles; a celebration of the first birthday of a landslide near Kratovo; and the swan lake protest in Orhid. These actions made the situation visible and helped bring about solutions.

However, street art actions can also address wider issues, such as personal data protection, disinformation threats, or corruption.

Changing views and perceptions

Some problems are treated as untouchable, while expert and activist explanations can struggle to reach a wider public. Artistic activism can bridge that gap through the accessibility of an artwork: A simple, readable form can make serious phenomena and policies easier to grasp, encouraging people to question views they may previously have accepted or failed to notice.

Some famous examples of street art activism in North Macedonia include “Sharks in the Vardar River,” which commented on the Skopje 2014 project; “The Eyes of the Trees,” about excessive tree-cutting in Skopje; the “Monument to Diazepam” to raise awareness about overuse of prescription drugs; the Ohrid trout’s speech for St. Nicholas Day; the giant nest carrying a message from birds; and the campaign for the referendum to save GTC, the historic public City Shopping Center in Skopje.

Using different approaches, these actions invited citizens to reconsider their views on public policies and decisions.

Encouraging public responses and broader engagement

Some actions aim to provoke responses and mobilize a range of actors. These include not only authorities and institutions, but also professional associations, specialist non-governmental organizations and other groups working on specific issues. At times, such groups may engage less often with the problems citizens face, because communication with communities is limited or because they are reluctant to leave their comfort zones.

The media play an important role in this process. Prompted by an action, they seek answers from different actors. When answers are not forthcoming, pressure grows on those actors to take the problem more seriously. In this way, public attention and media coverage can encourage wider engagement.

Early actions on air pollution in Skopje in 2010 and 2011 are one example. With media support, the group “Urban Art Actions” pressured environmental organizations to take air pollution more seriously.

A similar approach appears in “Bread for All” about poverty; “How Many More Victims?” about cyclist safety in Skopje; and more recent actions on river pollution (featuring a mobile statue of floating feces). In these cases, public pressure helped bring the issues to greater attention among organizations and the wider public.

Some of artistic activism’s effectiveness comes from the way actions are made. Preparation often takes place in a studio or garage. It requires serious effort, but can also be an engaging and creative process. Working this way may help people avoid some of the burnout associated with sustained activism, although it does not remove the pressures that can come with public action.

Another source of artistic activism’s effectiveness — and one reason it is becoming more visible in public communication — is its ability to make a problem difficult to ignore. When that happens, the political cost of inaction can rise. Authorities may begin to view a problem in terms of its potential effect on voters at the next election. If the cost of addressing it is lower than, or comparable to, the possible loss of votes, a response and a solution become more likely.

Written by Guest Contributor

articles.author: Adam Zewe | MIT News
articles.title: Q&A: How AI came to model the “messy” human mind
articles.excerpt: Assistant Professor Benjamin Lindquist studies how engineers deliberately injected randomness into early AI, giving rise to deep-learning models that sometimes hallucinate.
articles.content:
Adam Zewe | MIT News · MIT News · MIT News republication policy

Assistant Professor Benjamin Lindquist studies how engineers deliberately injected randomness into early AI, giving rise to deep-learning models that sometimes hallucinate.

Generative artificial intelligence models are rooted in ideas of mid-20th century engineers who thought some amount of irrationality was essential for a machine that could think like a human, contends Benjamin Lindquist, an assistant professor in the MIT History Section, who holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and is a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. 

To mimic creative thinking, these AI pioneers intentionally injected randomness into algorithms designed to deterministically solve problems, Lindquist writes in a new paper that appears in the journal Past and Present. In the paper, he traces the origins of AI hallucinations back to this early research and suggests there will be inevitable tradeoffs between creativity and predictability when trying to build machines that mimic human behavior. MIT News spoke with Lindquist about these ideas.

Q: Why did early computer engineers believe they needed to inject randomness and irrationality into AI systems designed for logic and calculation? 

A: There is a long history of many figures in the world of science and art theorizing that chance plays an important part in discovery and creativity — in the ability to originate ideas. They equated creativity with unexpected leaps of logic, or even a dream-like state that allows you to think about things from a new perspective. 

In the early 1950s, one popular idea from John Pierce, who was a prominent electrical engineer at Bell Labs, was about math being valuable in the world of art. The idea was shared by a lot of people working in early computing. When we think of artwork that includes math, we may think of something very orderly and precise, but Pierce came to the opposite conclusion. He concluded that the utility of math is that it could remove order from art. Then in a very calculated way, math could add a burst of the unexpected as a means to deviate from clichés and add an element of irregularity which just might lead to insight. 

One popular way to add irregularity into otherwise predictable computers was through artificial (or random) neural networks. Many early neural networks were built by psychologists, who thought that by enabling scientists to build a model of the brain, artificial neural networks allowed scientists to observe what is happening inside, including how brains make productive mistakes. Rather than being black boxes, researchers believed these systems could open this black box of the mind and let scientists peer inside and see all the messy stuff that was really happening.

But there was another camp in the world of AI who thought that creative thinking was just “normal” thinking done better. It is interesting to look at these two very simplistic heuristics for understanding intelligence and creativity, and how they do and don’t mesh. The debate, then, was about trying to determine what human inventiveness boils down to, and then how to reconstitute human inventiveness in machine form. 

Q: How did these early computer engineers view AI, and how is it different from the way we think about AI today?

A: When we think of AI systems, we think of ChatGPT or Claude. We value and use these systems because they give answers that, most of the time, are correct. One of the things that was most interesting to me in this research was finding out that a lot of the early advocates of these systems valued them for exactly the opposite reason. They wanted a system that, on occasion, gave answers that deviated from their expectations. They already had systems that could deliver reasonable and expected answers. They saw neural networks as valuable because they could give unexpected, perhaps even strange and bizarre answers.

One reason we might view these systems differently today could be because of how they operate. Early on, these systems were confined to laboratories, so there weren’t really any real-world consequences of a system that gives a strange, or wrong, output. But now there are legal and monetary reasons why OpenAI or Anthropic doesn’t want a chatbot that gives unexpected or creative answers. There has been a “sanding down” of strangeness in these systems. They still potentially have that at their core, but it is something that is now largely suppressed.

Q: How did early neural networks that incorporated randomness to simulate human creativity evolve to become the dominant paradigm in AI?

A: For a long time, a specific kind of AI called “symbolic AI” was the dominant approach. Essentially, symbolic AI says the world is based on rules. The role of the AI researcher is to try and reconstruct the knowledge of the world in facts and propositions and feed it into a computer.

Neural networks, with their use of randomness to solve problems, started to gain traction in the 1950s but fell out favor early on. Frank Rosenblatt, a psychologist who was a very important early figure in neural networks, died prematurely; he died accidentally on his 43rd birthday in 1971. He was quite a charismatic and forceful personality, who made a lot of grand promises about what systems based on neural networks could do. By the time he died, a shift toward symbolic AI was already underway. It is possible if, had he lived, things might have turned out differently.

But neural networks never went away. By the 1980s they had shifted more into the world of cognitive science. To become more powerful, and more useful, neural networks needed a lot of data and computational power. That didn’t really arrive until the advent of the internet, when a lot of data became available and computing started to power up. Around 2012, neural networks started to outperform and outpace a statistical form of machine learning, and they kept growing from there.

Q: What lessons can we learn from studying AI’s history that could inform its development? 

A: I think there is a cautionary lesson here. The ideas and experiences of these early engineers tell us that we can work toward quashing hallucinations — we can work toward making AI perform a certain way so it doesn’t produce unexpected or unwanted answers — but there are going to be other consequences of that. These historical figures were onto something. There is a connection between the surprising and creative conclusions AI can offer and errors or hallucinations. There are tradeoffs when we build our systems to behave one way or the other. Maybe it is impossible to be completely at either end of the spectrum, but when we work toward one thing robustly, we often sacrifice something else unintentionally.

articles.author: Global Voices Caribbean
articles.title: Riddims against copyright
articles.excerpt: The Caribbean has long been exploited on the world stage, and copyright law is no exception
articles.content:
This story by Global Voices Caribbean originally appeared on Global Voices. Text licensed under CC BY 3.0. Reformatted for reading; third-party media omitted.

The Caribbean has long been exploited on the world stage, and copyright law is no exception

By Alexis Hancock

“Oh! Bob Marley, right?” Jamaican culture has been popularised by the mainstream, and as a Jamaican-American, I often get a glimpse into how others have consumed it and from what point of view. I would not call myself an ardent Marley fan, but I know the kind of people who are most likely attached to his music outside of Jamaica — for example, the potential counterculture student of the 1970s at UCLA who found connection to his messages of resistance. 

My personal fascination with Jamaican music is the “riddim” — the Jamaican patois spelling of “rhythm” — an instrumental beat or tune constructed not for a single artist, but to be used by the collective of the time and to be both enjoyed and critiqued by the culture makers of Jamaican art: the disenfranchised masses. 

As a public interest technologist and digital rights advocate, I view the “riddim” with an open-source lens. It helped to protect Jamaican culture, particularly from Western constructs that are heavily embedded in existing power dynamics like rigid copyright laws and the corporate commodification of music.

Riddims

Dancehall’s interactive, collaborative nature doesn’t treat a work as isolated or even something that is “finished.” Iteration is a part of the creative process that is decided by the next function or party. In Larisa Kingston Mann’s “Rude Citizenship,” she outlines how copyright law was written at a time when many of the island’s people were themselves considered property under slavery, thereby creating — from the very start — a contentious relationship with those holding the society’s wealth. Copyright law was set up for those with ample resources to dictate what could be protected and who could profit.

Beat-sharing directly challenges neo-colonial copyright’s individualistic definition of ownership and originality. Traditional copyright promotes monopoly over expression, enforced by harsh legal mechanisms (such as statutory damages) that make intertextuality, reuse, and artistic experimentation legally risky. Even Sean Paul, one of the most commercially successful dancehall artists in the world, attributed his mainstream success of “Get Busy” to the Diwali Riddim. If not for this collective creativity and shared use, we would not see dancehall music evolve and get pushed to the world in the way that it has.

Collective sharing didn’t stop at just music; dance was often learned collectively as well. I used to watch “passa passa” videos in high school and college, just to learn and keep up to date with the latest dances coming out of Jamaica and New York City in the early 2000s. These parties were the bane of anyone entrenched in respectability. The clothes were outlandish, the manners “rude,” the dancehall queens nothing short of acrobatic, and the parties could go until 6:00 a.m. 

But this was also the time when new artists could get a slot, vendors could make a little money, and producers could collaborate with artists and get public consensus on what worked before dropping money at a studio.

Caribbean economics

The Caribbean has long been exploited on the world stage in many ways, and copyright law is no exception.

Jamaica was often sidelined into less than favourable international trade agreements that didn’t keep the interests of the Jamaican masses in mind. More often than not, there was a strict one-size-fits-all structure, dictated by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank: detrimental loan structures, one-sided economic trade agreements, currency devaluation, and exploitative labour guidelines. 

In 1992, the IMF created terms that heavily impacted Jamaica’s economy. This served as the backdrop for the Jamaica Copyright Act of 1993, when the country was directed to reshape its laws to participate in global trade. More rigid terms forced artists to start registering “riddims,” and while these laws are purported to protect artists, less resourced and independent artists struggled to make claims against large producers. This also killed the “handshake agreements” many artists and producers made prior to 1993.

Modern dancehall and beyond

This hasn’t stopped dancehall creators from organising alternative circuits of commerce and performance, social intimacy, and communal engagement. Even today, the continuous nature of dancehall works still causes friction with how copyright laws function. 

This year, a monumental copyright case was overturned by a U.S. federal judge who named many famous artists in a list of 150, and affected about 2,000 tracks. The plaintiffs, Cleveland “Clevie” Browne and the heirs of Wycliffe “Steely” Johnson, claimed that the “Fish Market” riddim (also known as the “Pocoman Jam riddim”) was the basis and source of the percussion pattern that runs through reggaeton, the now billion-dollar musical genre with origins in the Spanish reggae of Panama brought by  Afro-Jamaican migrants, and further magnified by Puerto Rican artists.

However, the logic was denied. As US District Judge André Birotte Jr. said, “Plaintiffs have not clearly identified what copyrighted work contains the allegedly protectable selection and arrangement they seek to enforce.”

The claim failed to take all selections and arrangements mentioned and tie them to one work. But rather, it referenced a collection of works that mirrored parts over time: “That principle is especially significant here. Skidmore cautioned that a plaintiff cannot ‘reconstitut[e] the copyrighted work as a combination of unprotectable elements’ and then claim that those elements are substantially similar because they appear in an accused work, even where the elements are presented in ‘a different aesthetic context.’”

The nature of riddims is a double-edged sword here. Browne and Johnson were deprived of a chance to share in the profits of their creativity that set the groundwork for a whole new genre of music. If this lawsuit had gone in their favour, the logic could potentially have put any new reggaeton artist to this profit-sharing standard, possibly resulting in conditions only well-backed artists like Bad Bunny could afford to accommodate. Such an outcome could have created a disempowering dynamic for new artists. A power structure riddims fought in the first place.

We can all easily hear the main percussion in Puerto Rican reggaeton and Dominican dembow, but copyright’s ears are selectively biased against rhythm — usually favouring money, the artist’s will to attribute credit to where it’s due, and when the tracks were created in the more popular artist’s career. In fact, Black artists are often credited much later for genre-defining work and after lighter-skinned artists have made their money.

Despite the mainstream push away from collective processes, dancehall continues to evolve. What “makes Jamaicans cool” is the layers of understanding that come with what we share. Copyright creates a stamp in time — a piece of “the cool” the mainstream can manage to freeze and sell. Yet, the true cool develops alongside the collective and remains protected by that shared understanding.

Written by Global Voices Caribbean

articles.author: Alex Shipps | MIT CSAIL
articles.title: This design software reimagines everyday objects as self-aware devices
articles.excerpt: “X-Hinges” helps design and 3D print items like lamps and gloves with an interactive twist: automatically embedded sensors that perceive and adaptively respond to human contact.
articles.content:
Alex Shipps | MIT CSAIL · MIT News · MIT News republication policy

“X-Hinges” helps design and 3D print items like lamps and gloves with an interactive twist: automatically embedded sensors that perceive and adaptively respond to human contact.

As a child, you likely saw a few Disney movies depicting inanimate objects, such as clocks, cups, and toys, as interactive companions to humans — an act of pure magic, seemingly. But scientists at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) are now doing something similar: transforming stationary items into self-aware tools that perceive and respond to human motion to complete a task.

Engineers have 3D-printed these dynamic items with built-in sensing, using conductive materials for sensors and traces (sort of like wires) inside. The issue: both components were typically fabricated using the same material, so they’d emit similar signals. It’s sort of like hearing two radio stations at the same time, a mixup that’s hard to interpret. This confuses, say, a glove that relays instructions to a robotic hand about how to handle a specific object. The device couldn’t filter out the noise or verify the angle of a user’s motions, leading a humanoid student to make errors.

Researchers at CSAIL and Tianjin University (TJU) in China may have found a way to 3D print more precise interactive items. With their “X-Hinges” software, users can customize a design, and the tool will automatically embed two different materials: a filament for the sensors designed to send the strongest signal possible, and another for the wire-like elements that don’t interfere. Interactions won’t get lost in translation, meaning users can fabricate objects that respond in real-time, such as small robots, household decor, object-detection systems, and toys.

With X-Hinges, users can put together an item by selecting and connecting different shapes, then choosing how certain parts move. The item won’t be limited to moving in just one way like previous approaches; instead, users can select up to three “axes:” compressing, up and down, or to the sides. Building a robotic hand, for example, you’d likely want its fingertips to move vertically and laterally. The new tool would then embed sensors where the object bends (in this case, its joints) to capture motion data from both angles. That way, the device can understand and respond to your interactions more dynamically once it’s 3D-printed.

“It’s kind of like adding a conscious element to everyday objects,” says Jiaji Li, MIT electrical engineering and computer science (EECS) postdoc and CSAIL researcher, who is a senior author on a paper introducing the work. “What you get is objects that better understand how they’re being used and have more ways to respond. In the same way an AI agent is programmed to make certain decisions based on our instructions, these creations have built-in sensing to adaptively react to human touch.”

Jiaji Li and lead author Xiang Chang, a TJU PhD student and visiting researcher at CSAIL, used X-Hinges to create many clever devices. For example, they made a glove that can teach a robot how to grasp blocks. It adjusts to the size of a user’s hands, then records how the joints in their fingers bend via sensors before rapidly relaying that information to a humanoid hand to mimic it. The glove could be useful in factories or homes, where a robot often needs to learn new interactions quickly.

The researchers also produced a small, origami-style lamp using X-Hinges. It senses when a human pinches it closed and adjusts its brightness accordingly. When you turn on this adaptive, portable light source (sort of like a reading light), it looks like a piece of folded-up paper that sprouts into a lamp.

X-Hinges can even assemble devices that identify which objects have been placed on it. You could put a banana on top, for instance, and it’ll recognize the fruit almost immediately based on the tactile data it’s recorded using its sensors. This advanced physical awareness could be integrated into detection systems in places such as airports and grocery stores. 

Behind each of the scientists’ creations is an easy-to-use interface that helps you design interactive objects from scratch. Users can choose how each part of their design looks and moves, just as the researchers did when making a video game controller that resembles a cartoon shark.

X-Hinges gives you four shapes to choose from: a custom option, cylinder, rectangle, and thin outline. To recreate the unique look of a shark’s tail, the researchers designed their own shape. They then chose how the toy bent, opting for its tail to move up and down, sort of like a joystick. Finally, the program embedded the sensors, and the scientists 3D-printed their device.

The researchers say that X-Hinges’ diverse motions are a novel feature compared to past attempts to 3D-print responsive everyday objects. “Most methods only allow for one axis of motion, often due to signal interference. X-Hinges enables your 3D-printed item to move from three angles,” says Chang. “Ultimately, you get a design with the intended movement you want. It also records motion data in each of those areas at the same time, making the device responsive to different kinds of interactions.”

The tool could help realize the untapped potential of the seemingly mundane. Objects we use every day for a specific purpose, like a water bottle for drinking or a lamp for lighting, could become interactive gadgets. Much like how a chatbot uses a sort of digital intelligence to answer your prompts, an object could leverage a kind of physical intelligence to execute a physical task when users interact with it.

For now, though, X-Hinges faces a calibration bottleneck. Each time an item is 3D-printed, its layout of electrical elements varies slightly, so two devices that appear identical from the outside may not make the same sensor readings. This is crucial if you’re building a deformable fitness glove, for instance, for two separate users. To fix this, Chang and Li built a computer vision system that can recalibrate outputs to align, ensuring data is accurate across two of the same items, although they hope to develop a built-in signal recalibration mechanism in the future.

That ambition traces back to the throughline in Jiaji Li’s own research: letting actuation and sensing “grow” directly inside a 3D-printed object, instead of adding them on afterward. He previously built printed tendon-driven mechanisms that gave objects the ability to move; X-Hinges is how he’s now building on the ability to sense. The next step, he says, is combining the two in a single print — it’s actuation and sensing born together in the same fabrication process, opening the door to new physical platforms for embodied intelligence and AI agents.

Chang and Li wrote the paper with MIT associate professor of EECS and CSAIL principal investigator Stefanie Mueller and recent TJU graduate Haiyang Yan. Their work was supported, in part, by a postdoctoral research fellowship from Zhejiang University and the MIT-GIST Program.

The researchers will present their work at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology in early November.

articles.author: Gabriela Mesones Rojo
articles.title: Venezuela faces a deepening energy crisis as protests grow
articles.excerpt: For most of the population, unreliable electricity has become a chronic part of daily life
articles.content:
This story by Gabriela Mesones Rojo originally appeared on Global Voices. Text licensed under CC BY 3.0. Reformatted for reading; third-party media omitted.

For most of the population, unreliable electricity has become a chronic part of daily life

This piece is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

“Yesterday we didn't have electricity for 11 hours. The day before, it was seven,” explains Yanira, a 33-year-old artist and designer who lives with her ailing 73-year-old father in Maracaibo, one of the cities most affected by Venezuela’s electricity rationing. In a region where temperatures remain high throughout much of the year, going without electricity is more than an inconvenience. For her family, the blackouts directly affect their health, work and daily routines.

And Yanira is not alone.

Across the country, increasingly long and unpredictable blackouts are disrupting work, education, businesses and sleep. In several cities, frustration has spilled into the streets, with residents protesting outages and blocking roads in the darkness.

In August, residents of various cities, including Turmero and Valencia, took to the streets at night to protest the worsening situation. Their demonstrations came as authorities expanded electricity rationing in response to growing pressure on the country’s fragile power grid.

The crisis is particularly severe outside Caracas, where scheduled outages lasting between six and 15 hours a day have been reported in several regions. Authorities have also introduced shorter working hours for some public sector employees, and reached an agreement with shopping malls to reduce electricity consumption.

The government has attributed the worsening shortages in part to the effects of El Niño, which has brought drought and unusually high temperatures to Venezuela. There is also, however, a series of factors worsening the situation, like the major failure at Guri Hydroelectric plant, where one of its turbines — which generated 770MW — collapsed.

The country’s electricity problems long predate the current weather conditions. Venezuela’s power system has suffered from years of underinvestment, poor maintenance and allegations of corruption, resulting in a system that is increasingly unable to meet the country’s electricity needs.

A crisis measured in lost hours

For residents of Maracaibo, one of Venezuela’s largest and most economically important cities, the crisis has become deeply personal. Yanira says she can spend at least six hours a day without electricity. The outages have affected both her livelihood and her mental health.

She has had a hard time finding a job or even working remotely, because blackouts make it difficult to function. She eventually began running small businesses from home, first selling sandwiches and cepillados zulianos — shaved-ice treats popular in the region — but keeping food frozen and drinks cold is a constant challenge when electricity can disappear without warning:

View this post on Instagram

The hardest moments come at night. Without air conditioning, sleeping becomes difficult in Maracaibo’s intense heat — and while opening the windows brings some relief, it also lets tropical insects inside. Yanira says the situation has affected her sleep so severely that she began taking sleeping pills.

Her experience reflects a broader problem. According to Venezuela’s 2025 Living Conditions Survey, only around 10 percent of Venezuelans live without experiencing power outages. For most of the population, unreliable electricity has become a chronic part of daily life.

The blackouts are also taking a toll on local economies. The National Chamber of Commerce reported that 38 percent of businesses had closed during the year, amid the combined effects of the electricity crisis and the country’s broader economic difficulties.

In Puertos de Altagracia which, like Maracaibo, is situated in Zulia state, Sara Hernández works at a company that sells bottled drinking water. Even with access to a generator, keeping the business running during outages is difficult because fuel is not always available. The uncertainty makes planning almost impossible. Electricity can disappear at any moment, and some businesses experience more than one rationing period in a single day.

The consequences extend beyond commerce. In Maracay, in Venezuela’s central region, resident Kellys Gallardo told El País that she receives daily text messages from the state electricity company, Corpoelec, warning her about planned outages, but the messages sometimes arrive only after the power has been cut.

Gallardo, who works at a company that manufactures printer ink cartridges, experiences outages both at work and at home. Her children are also affected when electricity rationing disrupts their schools.

From frustration to protest

As blackouts grow longer and less predictable, anger is becoming increasingly visible in public spaces. Residents who once endured outages quietly are now gathering in the streets, blocking roads and demanding solutions. In cities like Turmero, Valencia, El Tocuyo, Caja Seca, Calabozo, Zaraza and Valle de la Pascua, nighttime protests have highlighted how deeply the electricity crisis has entered everyday life.

The year 2026 saw a significant surge in both the frequency and widespread nature of civil unrest across Venezuela. The Observatorio Venezolano de Conflictividad Social (OVCS) documented upwards of 4,000 protests between January and August, a figure that OVCS coordinator Marco Antonio Ponce noted is triple the amount seen in earlier comparable timeframes. Daily demonstrations averaged 22 in August alone, with persistent electricity blackouts ranking among the public’s primary grievances.

For Venezuelans, the problem is about more than having to sit in the dark. It means businesses losing products and working hours, children having no electricity at school, families struggling to sleep in extreme heat, workers unable to plan their days, and people unable to access healthcare. In the Barquisimeto dialisis unit, for example, a lack of power left 42 kidney patients without treatment.

A problem that has lasted for years

Venezuela’s current electricity emergency echoes its 2019 crisis, when severe drought reduced water levels at the Guri reservoir, the hydroelectric complex that supplies a major share of the country’s electricity. One the most important events of this period was a 6six-day national blackout.

Today’s crisis is unfolding on top of years of deterioration in the electricity system. Venezuela has an installed generation capacity of approximately 30,000 megawatts, but currently produces less than half of that amount. The gap becomes particularly problematic during periods of high demand.

The government recently announced new investments aimed at rebuilding the system. In June, authorities signed an agreement with U.S.-based General Electric to restore 1,000MW of generating capacity over two years, with plans for an additional 5,000MW over the following four years.

Another agreement involving the Tocoma hydroelectric project, which began construction in 2007 but was never completed, was also announced. Authorities say these projects form part of a broader effort to recover Venezuela’s electricity infrastructure.

For residents living through the outages, however, long-term plans offer little immediate relief. In a country where electricity shortages have persisted for years, each new blackout carries the weight of a much longer story: one in which an essential public service has become increasingly unreliable, while residents are left waiting for the lights to come back on.

Written by Gabriela Mesones Rojo

articles.author: Alex Ouyang | Abdul Latif Jameel Clinic for Machine Learning in Health
articles.title: Why teaching AI about symmetry could make prenatal diagnosis more reliable
articles.excerpt: A model developed by researchers at MIT and Boston Children's Hospital adjusts scans on the fly to track fetal movement, potentially sparing families repeat hospital visits.
articles.content:
Alex Ouyang | Abdul Latif Jameel Clinic for Machine Learning in Health · MIT News · MIT News republication policy

A model developed by researchers at MIT and Boston Children's Hospital adjusts scans on the fly to track fetal movement, potentially sparing families repeat hospital visits.

Despite millions of years of evolution, the development of the human fetus remains a complex process that is vulnerable to genetic, environmental, and metabolic disruptions. These disruptions could result in developmental abnormalities, starting with one of the first organs to begin developing in the fetus that continues to develop after birth: the brain.

In a routine prenatal ultrasound, the sonographer will flag possible brain abnormalities for additional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). But imperfect imaging can result in missed or incorrect diagnoses. 

To assist with the early detection and treatment of these abnormalities, researchers at MIT, Boston Children’s Hospital, and Inria have developed and trained a deep learning model called E(3)-Pose that helps image the fetus’s head while it’s in motion to capture a high-resolution image that the radiologist can examine. A paper about the work was presented at the 2026 European Conference on Computer Vision. 

“One of the problems with having the baby move is that the slices are all over the place,” says first author Ramya Muthukrishnan. Muthukrishnan is an MIT PhD student in the lab of Sunlin (1966) and Priscilla Chou Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science Polina Golland, who is a principal investigator at the MIT Abdul Latif Jameel Clinic for Machine Learning in Health (Jameel Clinic) and the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL).

By slices, Muthukrishnan is referring to a series of 2D images taken during a fetal MRI scan. These 2D planes stacked together effectively make up one high-resolution, 3D image of the fetus’s head. But if the head shifts during imaging, each 2D image “slice” could end up being taken from a different angle, resulting in gaps in the final scan and unusual slice orientation. These problems may cause the physician reviewing the MRI to miss or incorrectly diagnose a pathology in the fetal brain.

“There are very fine details that you need a very good volumetric picture of the brain to see,” explains Muthukrishnan. “If you have coverage gaps, you can’t see critical regions, and you need to be able to see well to detect abnormal development.”

What makes E(3)-Pose particularly good at tracking fetal motion is its focus on physics. Rather than simply training the model to learn physics from the data, the very principles of physics are baked into the neural network: left-right symmetry of the fetal head is embedded in the model architecture, making it easier for the model to accurately identify the brain’s orientation. 

When Muthukrishnan began working on the project at the start of her PhD, she had no background in physics, let alone MRI physics. Most of her experience was in computer science. “I was surprised when I had to go and implement this on the scanner,” she recalls. “I was not prepared for how many times I would crash the scanner because putting things on hardware and getting it to work on hardware is a different beast than training a model to run on data on a GPU.” 

Despite the challenges, Muthukrishnan persisted. She remembers shadowing a radiologist who performed fetal MRI scans at Boston Children’s Hospital at the start of her PhD and observing the shared frustration of the patient and radiologist: the pregnant mother felt uncomfortable after spending an hour in an MRI, only to quit the scan halfway; the radiologist was unable to procure a full, high-quality MRI to monitor the development of the fetus.

“Seeing frustration about it helped me decide what I wanted to do with my PhD, because it felt like this was a pain point,” Muthukrishnan says.

Fortunately, she had help: Co-author Borjan Gagoski, an assistant professor of radiology at Harvard Medical School and a researcher at Boston Children's Hospital, developed a sequence that acquires additional MRI scans to assist with training E(3)-Pose and worked with Muthukrishnan to help troubleshoot the scanner whenever it crashed. Co-author and Boston Children’s Research Assistant Aryn Lee recruited the pregnant volunteers and assisted with acquiring each of the MRI scans. Senior authors who helped guide the project include Elfar Adalsteinsson, MIT professor of electrical engineering and computer science; Ellen Grant, the Käthe Beutler Professor of Pediatrics and professor of radiology at Harvard Medical School; and Golland. Benjamin Billot, a researcher at Inria and a former postdoc in Golland’s group, helped Muthukrishnan get started with the initial method he developed.

“Ramya’s work elegantly combines geometric concepts like equivariance and symmetry with the power of deep learning to change how MRI scanners acquire the images, and to ultimately help the physicians detect and treat problems early in development. It’s an impressive research project that is deep and fundamental in how it models image acquisition, with clear clinical impact,” says Golland.

Grant, who directs the Fetal Neonatal Neuroimaging and Developmental Science Center (FNNDSC) at Boston Children’s, adds that Muthukrishnan’s work “will automate fetal brain MRI, replacing today's slow, manual process with faster and more comfortable scans for mothers, while also providing higher-quality images for radiologists to interpret.”

E(3)-Pose’s applications could extend beyond motion tracking for fetal MRIs. It could assist with imaging other hard-to-image anatomy, and even autonomous driving applications, where limited sensors need to capture noisy, 3D data in order to track 3D objects.

For now, Muthukrishnan hopes to improve E(3)-Pose so that it can help with imaging second-trimester or younger fetuses, as the model is primarily trained on third trimester fetuses. Second-trimester fetuses are “so small, they move around a lot more because there’s more space in the uterus,” Muthukrishnan says. “They’re more important to focus on because the earlier you detect brain abnormalities, the easier it is to intervene.” 

This work is supported by the MIT Jameel Clinic, the MIT Takeda Program, the Chou Family Transformative Research Fund, the National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering, and the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development.

articles.author: Jocelyn Falempe
articles.title: Modernizing the console with kmscon
articles.excerpt: For decades, the Linux virtual console has relied on the kernel fbcon driver, to draw the framebuffer, to manage fonts, and to handle keyboard layout. Starting with Fedora 45, we’re switching to a userspace utility called kmscon. Depending on your usage of virtual console, this may impact your workflow.
articles.content:
Jocelyn Falempe · Fedora Magazine · CC BY-SA 4.0

For decades, the Linux virtual console has relied on the kernel fbcon driver, to draw the framebuffer, to manage fonts, and to handle keyboard layout. Starting with Fedora 45, we’re switching to a userspace utility called kmscon. Depending on your usage of virtual console, this may impact your workflow.

If you’re not a developer or a system administrator, chances you probably never heard about fbcon or virtual terminal (VT), in this case you’re probably not impacted.

You can still read the rest if you’re curious about minimal text interfaces, and maybe you’ll start using it.

How to use the virtual console

Most of the graphic sessions runs in tty1 or tty2. So press Ctrl+Alt+F3 to switch to tty3, and you will get a login prompt. This is the virtual console we’re talking about. To go back to your graphic session, press Ctrl+Alt+F1 (or F2 or F7 depending on your desktop environment).

Why is kmscon replacing fbcon ?

The legacy fbcon driver runs directly in the kernel space, and has significant drawbacks:

  • Security: Each bug in fbcon can be exploited in the kernel directly, and each crash is a kernel panic.
  • Keyboard layout: The keyboard layouts supported by the kernel are different from what userspace is using. So when you choose the keyboard layout in the anaconda installer, it tries to find the kernel layout that is as close as possible to the chosen layout.
  • Fonts: fbcon only uses bitmap fonts, which look small on a High DPI display, and you can’t resize them at runtime. They have limited unicode support. Kmscon can use freetype, and render all monospace fonts.
  • Scrolling: fbcon does not support scrolling anymore, due to a CVE.
  • Mouse: fbcon does not have mouse support, it can be added with gpm, but is a bit clumsy. Kmscon uses a transparent hardware cursor when available, and has basic mouse support.
  • Fbdev: fbcon relies on the old fbdev interface, but all GPU drivers are now using drm. Switching to kmscon allows dropping the fbdev emulation layer in the kernel.

What this will change for users and administrators ?

  • Kmscon uses pseudo-tty (pts) devices. So when you run tty it returns /dev/pts/0 instead of /dev/tty1, like when you use a graphic terminal. So you will need to update all scripts or configuration that use this information.
  • Kmscon uses the exclusive drm interface to the GPU to draw the terminal. If you want to run a graphic session or a program that wants to use the GPU, it won’t work like it used to with fbcon. The reason is that fbcon runs in the kernel and can let any userspace application take the GPU. Kmscon can’t do that, so you have to tell it to release the GPU. This is done with a script called kmscon-launch-gui. For example, to start a graphic session you can run
    kmscon-launch-gui kmscube -c 100
    or
    kmscon-launch-gui startx
  • Kernel messages: By default the kernel error/warning messages are visible in tty1. It can be annoying when it mixes with what you are typing. You can read the messages with dmesg -w, or have a dedicated tty that runs
    kmscon --vt=%I --no-switchvt --oneshot --login -- dmesg -w
  • Kernel fonts: The setfont command has no effect on kmscon. Kmscon uses the built-in unifont or freetype if it’s available. You can read below how to configure it. kmscon can also use psf fonts, if you want the exact same looking as fbcon.
  • Keyboard layout: The loadkeys command has no effect on kmscon. Instead, kmscon listens to localectl dbus, and updates the keyboard layout accordingly. So, to change layout, run
    localectl set-keymap us
  • Kmscon replaces the default console in F45, for tty1-6. If you want to keep a tty using fbcon, just in case, you can run
    sudo systemctl mask kmsconvt@tty5 && sudo systemctl enable --now getty@tty5
    Then pressing Ctrl+Alt+F5 switches to your good old fbcon console.

Default kmscon shortcuts

  • Zoom in: Ctrl++, Ctrl+WheelUp
  • Zoom out: Ctr+-, Ctl+WheelDown
  • Rotate the terminal: Super++, Super+-
  • Scroll up: Shift+UpArrow, Shift+PageUp, Mouse Wheel Up
  • Scroll down: Shift+DownArrow, Shift+PageDown, Mouse Wheel Down
  • Copy/paste: select with the mouse, or select a word with double click, and MiddleClick to paste
  • Switch to ttyX: Ctrl+Alt+FX
  • Restart kmscon on ttyX: sudo systemctl restart kmsconvt@ttyX
  • To know on which VT you are using, echo $XDG_VTNR

How does it look ?

Previous experience, Fedora 45 with fbcon:

Fedora 45 with kmscon (unifont)

Fedora 45 with kmscon (freetype) and some customization (fish, Hack Nerd Font)

How to configure kmscon the way you like

Plugins

kmscon is split into multiple subpackages, so you have a minimal installation without graphic/font dependencies for servers, and optional packages for more features.

  • kmscon: main package, contains the unifont font, for good unicode support without additional dependencies.
  • kmscon-freetype: Use the freetype library to render the fonts.
  • kmscon-pango: Uses the pango library to render the fonts, it is deprecated in favor of kmscon-freetype.
  • kmscon-gl: This is an opengl renderer. This might be faster but also a bit blurry. You need to add hwaccel to your configuration file to actually use it.

Configuration file

The configuration file for kmscon is /etc/kmscon/kmscon.conf
you can copy the example with this command:
sudo cp /etc/kmscon/kmscon.conf.example /etc/kmscon/kmscon.conf

Here are the most common options to change:

verbose: enable more logs, if you have issues with kmscon. To get the logs, use
journalctl -u kmsconvt*

font-engine: defaults to freetype (if available) or unifont (fallback). You can also use pango, or psf (the format used by the kernel fonts)

font-name: The name of the font (for pango, freetype, and psf). As kmscon runs as root, the font must be installed in /usr/share/fonts, not in your home directory. You can find the exact name to use with fc-list. You can install Cascadia fonts, that are good for non-latin languages with
sudo dnf install cascadia-fonts-all
If you want fancy icons, Nerd fonts are good, but not available in the default Fedora repository. For psf font, font-name is the path to the font file.

font-size: The font height in pixels. By default kmscon tries to scale the font to have about 120×40 characters.

multi-monitor: multi-monitor configuration, the terminal is the same on all monitor. The default is scaled which will scale the font to avoid too much black border. Other options are clone, which will center the terminal on each monitor, and largest which will only use the largest monitor.

dpms-timeout: The timeout (in second) after which the monitor will be turned off. default to 600 (10 minutes). 0 means disabled.

no-mouse: This disable the mouse support. It can be useful to disable touchpad on some laptops.

palette: Change the default color palette for your terminal. You can define each color if none of the provided default palette suits you.

Conclusion

We hope you will enjoy using kmscon in Fedora 45. You may use it occasionally, or use it as your main session for some specific usage, like Veronica Explains for a writerdeck https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E7vFdy4BEAY.

If you encounter any bugs, have feature ideas, or want to contribute to development, the upstream repository is at https://github.com/kmscon/kmscon.
